participation.text: A royal moral and administrative message addressed different regional audiences; reception cannot be assumed.

evidence.text: Contemporary inscriptions offer a royal voice; later genealogies disagree about subsequent rulers.

coordination.text: Royal messages assigned practical and moral tasks to officials and subjects. Provision, communication and enforcement each required people; their outcomes need local evidence.

name: Ashoka: messages carved in stone
place: South Asia; locator at Sarnath, one pillar site
geographicPrecision: One inscription-site context; messages were distributed across a much wider area.

interval.label: Ashoka, c. 268–232 BCE
interval.note: Reign convention used by Neelis. Other chronologies place accession earlier; not exact dates for every edict.

question: What changes when a ruler speaks to people in different languages?
summary: Ashoka’s rule depended on people carrying, interpreting and acting on messages across regions. Rock and pillar inscriptions address moral conduct, officials and religious communities in different settings. They announce practical actions as well as ideals, but an announcement is not an inspection of its results. Reading selected edicts beside their places and audiences shows how royal government sought to work, and whose experiences still need other evidence.

sections.title: A message needed a local audience
sections.text: Neelis describes regional Prakrit inscriptions and Greek and Aramaic material at Kandahar. Language and script are separate choices. Neither proves that everyone nearby could read the message; hearing and explanation are further questions. The geographic distribution shows attention to different audiences. It does not outline every territory controlled by the Mauryas or trace one messenger’s journey.

sections.title: The announced actions were practical
sections.text: In Hultzsch’s English edition, Girnar Rock Edict II describes provision for people and cattle, planting useful herbs and digging wells and planting trees along roads. These are tasks requiring materials, people and continuing access, rather than an abstract slogan about kindness. Yet the royal statement alone does not identify every worker, demonstrate that every well was maintained or show how benefits were distributed. An account of implementation would need evidence from particular places and later use.

citations.locator: Printed pp. 3–4, Girnar II, sections A–D

sections.title: Officials were told how to exercise power
sections.text: Dhauli Separate Edict I addresses judicial officials at Tosali. The translated text asks for impartial treatment and warns about anger, haste, fatigue and other obstacles to good judgment. This gives a concrete mechanism for royal instruction: address the people making decisions and tell them how their work should change. It also preserves the king’s paternal authority over subjects. It is not a grant of equal political participation, a record of every judgment or proof that abusive treatment stopped.

sections.title: Conquest and moral instruction belong together
sections.text: Rock Edict XIII expresses remorse over Kalinga’s conquest. The resulting account should keep warfare and the king’s moral presentation visible together, rather than turn remorse into proof that power no longer involved coercion. Neelis distinguishes the broader moral and administrative program of dhamma from a complete statement of Buddhist doctrine. Ashoka patronized Buddhist institutions and also supported other religious communities. Different inscriptions and audiences offer a more useful history than treating every carved message as one identical manifesto.

returnPrompt: What evidence from one named locality could test a royal announcement about provision or fair treatment?

deeperReading.title: The message at Dhauli is not the whole series
deeperReading.text: The 1925 edition distinguishes the two Separate Edicts at Dhauli and Jaugada from the Major Rock Edicts found in other versions. Those local sets substitute the Separate Edicts for XI–XIII. The map therefore does not put the well-known remorse passage from XIII onto the Dhauli rock. A place, a version and an individual passage must stay connected. Hultzsch’s editorial English also belongs to 1925; it is not the language that an ancient audience saw on the stone. Later discoveries at Kandahar need the separate modern source used here.

deeperReading.title: Instructions let us ask about reception
deeperReading.text: An order directed at officials can be unusually revealing about the difficulties a ruler wanted to address. A warning against hurry suggests an administrative concern, but it does not tell us how often decisions were rushed. The king’s claim to care for subjects is similarly different from a subject’s own account of treatment. To deepen this inquiry, seek regional archaeological evidence, inscriptions in their linguistic settings and accounts that can test access and enforcement. Later religious narratives should retain their own dates and purposes, rather than be inserted as eyewitness reports of the reign.

familyActivity.title: Match a message to its work
steps: Find Girnar, Dhauli and Kandahar on the map. Match them with practical provision, instructions to officials or regional language.
Choose one announced task. Name a person who would have to do something for it to happen.
Finish: “The inscription announces ___; to find out what happened, I would look for ___.”
familyActivity.explanation: A named place and a royal instruction are starting evidence. They do not show that every subject heard the same words or experienced the promised result.

evidenceReading.title: Read a royal instruction in its own setting
evidenceReading.introduction: These are paraphrases from a published English edition and a modern institutional synthesis; no ancient passage is silently assigned to a different rock.

items.label: Girnar II announces material provision
items.text: The translated edict describes useful planting, wells and trees along roads, as well as provision for people and cattle.
items.interpretation: Its verbs express the ruler’s account of action. They do not count functioning facilities or independently establish their reach.

items.label: Dhauli Separate I addresses officials
items.text: The translated instruction addresses judicial officials at Tosali and warns against anger, hurry and fatigue in their work.
items.interpretation: This is a particular message to an administrative audience. It does not supply every subject’s view of justice or a measured change in outcomes.

items.label: A regional set differs from another set
items.text: Dhauli and Jaugada carry two Separate Edicts in place of Major Rock Edicts XI–XIII.
items.interpretation: The Kalinga remorse passage of XIII should not be labelled as the text on the selected Dhauli rock. Language, version and location need separate checks.

review.reviewer: Codex source consultation and self-review; not independent historian approval
review.scope: Bounded C3 explanation with main/deeper/evidence reading, family entry, distinct reference phases and sourced geographic orientation.
limitations: The selected Hultzsch passages were read in OCR and specified original scans; no full edition, original-language or complete inscription-site audit claimed.
The 1925 edition predates the Kandahar material. Neelis supplies the separate language context. Translation choices and newer scholarship need further review.
Implementation, local reception, workers’ voices and coercion require more regional evidence.

placeStudy.title: Ashoka: regional audiences and different messages
placeStudy.description: Selected inscription settings and a capital orientation. The map distinguishes a geographic distribution from a territorial outline or messenger’s route. The main atlas locator at Sarnath is one pillar-site context; these points examine other settings.

points.label: Pataliputra — royal centre
points.text: Neelis identifies Pataliputra, near modern Patna, as a Mauryan capital. A royal centre does not establish the place where every inscription was drafted or heard.

points.label: Kandahar — Greek and Aramaic material
points.text: Neelis discusses Greek and Aramaic inscriptions here in the northwestern regional setting. This evidence is not supplied by the 1925 edition, which predates the discoveries.

points.label: Girnar — Rock Edict II
points.text: The Girnar version announces practical provision, planting and wells. This point locates the inscription setting; it does not map every facility named in the royal claim.

points.label: Dhauli — Separate Edict I
points.text: The local Separate Edict addresses judicial officials at Tosali. Do not transfer the remorse passage of Major Rock Edict XIII to this rock; the local set substitutes different messages.
